one_liner: EA's non-COW, SSO basic_string and inline-buffer fixed_string; beat the VC++ 7.1 Dinkumware string on push_back and swap.
what_it_does: eastl::basic_string<T, Allocator> (eastl::string, string16, string32) mirrors the std::basic_string interface and adds sprintf, set_capacity, force_size and tolower/toupper members, a named stateful allocator, and builds without exceptions. eastl::fixed_string<T, nodeCount, bEnableOverflow = true> is a basic_string whose allocator is an inline buffer of nodeCount characters (terminator included); with overflow enabled it spills to the heap, without it exceeding capacity is undefined behaviour or an allocation exception. Neither is std::string, so code that passes strings across library boundaries has to copy or use string_view.
how_it_is_fast: Today's string keeps a short-string buffer inside the 24-byte (64-bit) three-word object: 23 chars for char, 11 for char16_t, 5 for char32_t. It never does copy-on-write, uses raw pointers as iterators, hand-inlines begin()/size() for debug builds, has no char_traits layer, and grows capacity by 2x. fixed_string avoids heap allocation altogether while it fits. The published EASTL 0.96 gains (push_back 10-14x, swap 3.5x) were measured on the 0.96 implementation against the Dinkumware VC7.1 string, not on this layout.
when_to_use: Game, console or embedded code that already builds against EASTL and wants one string type with named allocators and exceptions disabled
Debug builds where std::string overhead hurts: the VC7.1 Debug table shows char push_back 8.95x and iteration 11.05x over the Debug std::string (but find 0.26x)
Bounded-length strings (names, paths, keys) kept inside an object or on the stack: fixed_string with a nodeCount that covers the common case
You need set_capacity/force_size-style control over the buffer, such as writing into it with a C API and then fixing the size
when_not_to_use: Expecting a speedup over today's libstdc++, libc++ or MSVC std::string: no published comparison against them exists, and the baselines measured were the VC++ 7.1 Dinkumware string, STLport and GCC 4.1 libstdc++; against STLport (Release) most rows were 1.00x and char16_t compare and swap were slower (0.82x, 0.90x)
Substring-search-heavy code: find(p, pos, n) is a plain eastl::search loop; char find was 0.74x against the VC++ 7.1 Dinkumware string in Release and 0.26x in Debug
Code that mostly talks to std::string APIs: every crossing copies, and fixed_string is a different type again because its allocator is a template argument
Small fixed_string with overflow enabled (roughly nodeCount 12 or less for char on 64-bit): the open overflow bug #454 corrupts the contents (see gotchas)
Wide characters needing long inline strings: SSO holds only 11 char16_t or 5 char32_t

integration.dependencies: EABase (CMake FetchContent); in the default configuration the application must define EASTL's two operator new[] overloads (doc/FAQ.md Info.15)
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (CMakeLists.txt: cxx_std_14); the benchmark suite does not compile with C++20 char8_t enabled (benchmark/CMakeLists.txt)
integration.platforms: any; the SSO flag bit is the MSB of the capacity on little-endian and the LSB on big-endian targets
integration.thread_safety: doc/FAQ.md: like std containers, a string instance is not safe for concurrent modification; reads from several threads are fine; a shared allocator needs its own locking
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the std::basic_string member set is mostly present, but it is a different type (no char_traits, size_type is eastl_size_t, substr copies the allocator), reserve never shrinks, and the char* constructor is implicit unless EASTL_STRING_EXPLICIT is set

gotchas: fixed_string overflow bug, issue #454 (open since 2021-12-17, no maintainer reply): fixed_string starts in the heap layout, so when a small one grows to a new capacity that still fits the SSO buffer, set_capacity takes its 'heap->sso' shrink path, copies n = new-capacity characters out of the smaller inline buffer (an out-of-bounds read) and sets the size to n; the HEAD code still has that path. fixed_string<char, 8> appended one char at a time stops at 'abbbbbb' in the issue's repro.

fixed_string::swap uses fixed_swap, which moves contents instead of swapping pointers and, for objects of EASTL_MAX_STACK_USAGE bytes or more, heap-allocates a temporary; comparing a fixed_string with nullptr segfaults in CharStrlen (issue #546, open).

reserve(n) never shrinks (C++20 semantics); use set_capacity or shrink_to_fit to release memory. The char* constructor is implicit by default, so passing a literal to a const string& parameter builds a temporary (doc/Gotchas.md).

Harness behind the published rows (benchmark/source/BenchmarkString.cpp, today's version): the 7-element pattern arrays pFind1_8/pFind1_16 have no terminating zero but go to insert(pos, const T*), which runs CharStrlen past the array (undefined behaviour); a guard that is true only on MinGW with non-Clang compilers skips the pattern insert into the std::basic_string<char16_t>, so on MSVC, GCC/Linux and Clang the char16_t find, rfind, *_of and compare rows search different strings; the reserve rows reward ignoring shrink requests; and each row is one timed loop with no repeats.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it if you are already on EASTL and want a whole std-like string family (string, fixed_string, string16/32) with custom allocators and no exceptions. For a single fixed-capacity string without EASTL, ETL's etl::string offers the same inline-buffer idea with a truncation flag instead of a heap spill; for faster number-to-string or comparison helpers, to_static_string or MengRao/str target those operations directly.
verified_claims_summary: doc/Benchmarks.md (EASTL 0.96, Windows x86, VC++ 7.1 Release, PPMalloc, no CPU model) times one loop per operation on strings pre-sized to 16 characters: against the Dinkumware string, push_back was 10.41x (char) and 14.30x (char16_t) faster and swap 3.48x, reserve 10.73x and 4.87x only because EASTL ignores shrink requests, while char find (0.74x) and compare (0.82x) were slower. EASTL's own times for identical code differ between the Dinkumware and STLport tables by up to 1.72x (char16_t compare 251,985,824 vs 432,760,228 cycles; find 165,298,157 vs 225,830,975), as large as many of the claimed ratios (derived from page data).
status_note: EASTL is actively maintained (BSD-3-Clause, 9.4k stars), but its string evidence is a single-run EASTL 0.96 table against Dinkumware/STLport. This enrichment found harness flaws the verifier did not record: an out-of-bounds read from unterminated pattern arrays, a MinGW-only guard that leaves the std char16_t string without the search pattern, and up to 1.72x run-to-run drift in EASTL's own timings. fixed_string carries an open heap-to-SSO overflow corruption bug (#454).
